summary: The smallest unbounded and dominating families of natural-number functions obey cardinal and cofinality bounds.
abstract: A function can eventually exceed every member of a countable collection of natural-number functions, allowing each member its own finite set of exceptions. The bounding number measures the smallest size of a collection for which no single eventual bound exists. The dominating number measures the smallest size of a collection whose members together eventually bound every natural-number function. Both numbers are uncountable and no larger than the size of the real line, with the bounding number no larger than the dominating number. The bounding number is regular: it cannot be approached in fewer stages than its own size. The dominating number needs at least that many stages as well. Under the continuum hypothesis, both are the first uncountable cardinal.
